To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a diffusive instability in a mite system is possible if (1) the mite predator has a sufficiently large dispersal motility, (2) it is sufficiently temperature-dependent, (3) its population density is large, and (4) its prey is sufficiently temperature-dependent and its population density is also large.

the predator's dispersal motility advantage and the prey's aggregative preytactic behavior can lead to a supercritical bifurcation of the uniform steady state to a family of parallel striped patterns, which can be interpreted as a model of clumping behavior.
the predator's motility advantage and the preytactic tendency to aggregate are sufficient conditions for the formation of spatially inhomogeneous patterns.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) What is the role of temperature in determining the population structure of a mite predator on a fruit tree? (ii) What are the possible effects of the dispersal motility of the predator on the population structure of the prey?

the following question. Can a one-dimensional model for a temperature dependent predator-prey interaction exhibit a subcritical bifurcation from an equilibrium state to spatially periodic patterns of a parallel stripe type?
the formation of spatial patterns by diffusive instability in a one-dimensional model for a mite system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the model system, in its present form, is capable of generating a variety of spatial patterns, including those with parallel stripes, which are in good qualitative agreement with experimental observations of the spatial patterns of phytophagoid arthropod populations on fruit trees.
the model is capable of generating spatially periodic patterns of a stripe type.
the model system is capable of exhibiting a rich and varied spectrum of one- and two-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the predator's motility and aggregating tendency can be sufficient to cause a spatially inhomogeneous distribution of the predator and its prey.

, for a given set of parameters, the model predicts that the predator-prey mites will form a pattern of parallel stripes in the critical interval, and the stripe width is determined by the temperature and by the dispersal advantage of the predator.

, in the absence of dispersal and preytactic aggregation, the system is always stable; however, the presence of these two factors may lead to instability, and the system may exhibit a family of stable parallel stripes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the predator-prey system can generate spatial patterns in the presence of a temperature gradient and that the resulting patterns may be quite different in different temperature intervals.

the interplay of temperature and population density can lead to the formation of spatial structures, and that the resulting patterns are sensitive to the relative values of the dispersal rates of the predator and prey species.
the presence of a sufficiently high dispersal rate for the predator can result in a subcritical bifurcation, which is a feature of a predator's having a dispersal motility advantage.
